title: 2026 Bespoked Dresden Picks 04: Curve, Mura, Norka, Quokka, Rasch – Paul Kalifatidi
content:
Guten morgen! We’re back in Saxony at the Flughafen Dresden for the 2026 Bespoked Dresden showcase. Paul and John spent the weekend at the world’s largest framebuilder showcase, selecting bikes to document for The Radavist’s coverage of the event. Check out our picks 04 from Curve, Mura, Norka, Quokka, and Rasch below!

The Radavist thanks Brooks England for sponsoring our 2026 Bespoked Dresden coverage and our independent Reportage!

Curve Cycling 00Kev – Paul Kalifatidi

When I first got into bikes, circa 2018, I quickly discovered Curve. Many years later, when I was shopping for a new bike, I heavily considered their GMX+, but the great bike shortage of 2021 made that impossible. Regardless, I paid close attention to the brand. Finally, at Bespoked Dresden, I was able to shake the hand of Jimmy Röstlund, the man behind the design of Curve’s bikes.

Curve brought a few bikes to Dresden, including their new 32″ BigKev, but I felt most drawn to their crazy carbon bike, the new 00Kev. The name is fun, and hints at the brand’s history as well as the construction of the bike. Like a few of the bikes I have documented, 00Kev features BONDed construction: carbon tubes glued into 3d printed titanium lugs. The name is also a nod to Curve’s first shop that was located on Bond Street.

00Kev is a race bike, through and through. Though I don’t do bike races, I do love riding as hard as possible and have a soft spot for this phenotype. I discussed this with Jimmy and mentioned that the bike ride I do most frequently is basically a two-hour sprint. I’ve had the privilege of reviewing a few bikes that fit this type of ride quite well, and they all feature big tire clearance and race-focused geometry.

Given its speedy demeanor, 00Kev has some wild numbers. As photographed, it features 2.4-inch tire clearance and can clear a 50-tooth chainring with standard gravel q-factor and hub spacing. The example pictured features Alugear’s 48-tooth chainring and crankset. Jimmy and I both debated whether such a giant chainring is even necessary, but a few of their sponsored riders are capable of turning such a ring with tires that big. Again, 00Kev is a race tool, not a bike that toddles.

I really like this bike, and I especially like how it photographed in the tunnel I was using all weekend. The glass walls cast a bluish tint that I corrected for while editing, but it really pulled out the blue notes used in the finish of the carbon fiber tubes of this bike. Jimmy, thank you for nerding out with me!

@CurveCycling

Mura Cycling Clothes – Paul Kalifatidi

This was maybe my favorite use of my photo stick of the weekend, so thank you, Markéta, for being silly with me. Markéta Kopcová owns Mura clothing. She cuts and sews stunning clothes in Brno, Czech Republic. At the show, she had a wide variety of her offerings. I went home with new pants and two fresh shirts, and I’ll be posting a review in the coming months. For now, let’s take a look at Markéta’s stunning work.

Mura’s catalog is constantly changing – the perks of being a small business. For the show, Markéta brought a blend of on-bike and off-bike apparel. Currently, her focus is on women’s riding wear, and when she has time, she’ll work on Men’s bibs too. The jerseys that she has featured a lovely printed fabric; every single one is unique.

Markéta focuses on using natural fabrics and blends. The shirts are custom dyed by her and feature prints from her graphic designer friend, are wool. After buying one, I lived in it for the tail end of the weekend and my giant travel day back to the United States. I loved it, and look forward to reviewing it alongside the pants and base layer I bought for Saturday night’s rave.

Markéta, thank you for making such stunning clothes; I’m still enthralled! You got Cari’s attention last year, so we’re going to have to send another person next year to keep the theme going.

@MuraCycling

Norka Negu – Paul Kalifatidi

When I met Norbert Toth, who goes by Norka, I did not expect to feel so emotionally attached to the frame of a bike I didn’t own. Whenever I explain the difference between a framebuilder and one of the giant brands to someone who might not understand the distinction, this is now going to be the story I reference.

Norka is friends with the owner of Ciclos La Ferro, a shop in his home of Bilbao, Spain. As the name suggests, they only sell metal bikes. Sadly, the shop dog, a German Shepherd named Negu, passed away. Norka immortalized the pooch through a bespoke bicycle. For a year, he worked on it. Custom and caring take time, and this is the greatest example of it that I have seen.

The most touching detail is that the lugs were modeled after Negu’s snout and ears. The paint scheme matches Negu’s own colors. Even the dropouts are inspired by Negu. I was beyond moved. Norka’s work is one of the finest examples of individual creativity and capability that seems to be almost ubiquitous in the European framebuilder scene.

He made everything for this frame: lugs, dropouts, fork crown, and stem. I joked that he didn’t make hydraulic disc brakes, and he laughed, because he wants to and thinks he could. That right there said everything I needed to know. Norka is a master at his craft and looks at technical challenge as a tantalizing moment for self-expression rather than a hurdle that needs to be overcome.

Norka, I would love to see disc brakes with your careful and delightful aesthetic. Please, keep up the fantastic work. I haven’t met any other person who puts so much careful consideration into the minutiae as you.

@NorkaBizi

Quokka Cycles Pilgrim and 27.5+ MTB – Paul Kalfatidi

There is always one builder that seems to steal the show, even if they don’t take home an award. Every single framebuilder at Bespoked Dresden was talking about the bikes from Quokka, and that might be greater praise than any single award. I know lots of 25-year-olds, given my own proximity to the age, and I don’t know any artists as talented as Brivaël, the man behind the French brand.

Brivaël named his bicycle company Quokka for some great reasons. His parents own a kangaroo sanctuary, so he has been around marsupials for most of his life. The Quokka is the cutest of them all, and he hopes that every single person that rides his bikes smiles like a Quokka.

I spent maybe 20 minutes just walking around his yellow breakaway bike before I even started taking photos. There are seemingly an infinite amount of angles and details to notice. Even after I thought I had seen everything, Brivaël pointed out the cable guides on the chainstay. That theme continued for the next hour. The Pilgrim is meant to travel. Brivaël was inspired to make it after hearing about Paragon’s closure. He wanted to use their coupler before it potentially was unavailable. He opted to only use one, on the downtube, and create his own breakaway solution for the top tube. The seatpost acts as a pin, holding the top tube and chainstays to the seat tube. Again: the theme of European experimental design on display.

Once I was done photographing and admiring the yellow bike, he showed me the blue bike. The two are entirely different, and yet the artistry within both of them is easily recognizable as Brivaël’s. Creating a consistent aesthetic, one that stands apart from the crowd, is a challenge. I’d compare Quokka to Drust, in that regard. I loved the blue bike and could easily see myself bounding through the woods on one, smiling like a marsupial the whole time.

Brivaël, thank you for your art and camaraderie. I hope to see you again soon!

@QuokkaCycles

Rasch Cycles Mom’s Bike and Ceramics Trailer – Paul Kalifatidi

I appreciated just how many European builders were proud to display practical bikes. Here, bikes are not always playthings; they are tools to live a better and healthier life. There was no better example than this bike and trailer built by Kata of Rasch Cycles. It’s the first frame she ever made, the first bike trailer she ever made, and it’s for her mother. It is a shining example of the ethos that bikes can change lives and contribute to a better and more connected world.

It is actually the first frame she ever made and the same one that she displayed at Bespoked Manchester in 2025. Kata dedicated the first bike she ever built for her mother. At one point, I asked if she would ever move away from Berlin, and she said: “No, I love my parents so much and want to be close.”

That’s cute as hell, but it gets better. Since the Manchester show, Kata’s mother has been riding the bike, but not as often as she wanted to. She is a talented ceramicist and felt forced to drive her car in order to transport ceramics and supplies to and from her studio. She doesn’t like driving, so Kata made her a trailer with a cargo fork to match. Behold, a beautiful blue trailer and its corresponding bicycle.

The bike is as practical as it gets, with the only luxury touch being a stunning red Brooks B17, and most importantly, Kata’s precision building skills. The framebag is made by Gramm Tourpacking, with whom Kata and Konstantin Drust share a workshop. It matches the hot pink accents hidden in the red frame finish. Shimano supported Kata by providing the utilitarian Cues drivetrain.

The trailer is stunning. It features a mesmerizing blue and bronze powder coat that John and I mistook for torch blueing. A dynamo-powered rear light is a thoughtful touch as well. It’s the first bespoke trailer that I have paid attention to, and I love the idea. Frankly, I’m more interested in making this than a bicycle, at least for the moment. My friend keeps trying to get me to build a frame, but if he is reading this, he might shortly get a text to make a canoe trailer for the canoe I don’t yet own. Kata, thank you for contributing to my bad ideas. It seems like you have a knack for helping people catch the building bug.

I want to finish this roundup on the highest note, one that you might have already inferred from the lead-in images: John judged the “Best New Builder” category and fittingly awarded Kata with the prize. Kata is, yes, new to framebuilding, but already she’s helping other women join her. She has started teaching classes and sharing her workshop space with women interested in this life.

John and everyone else at the show couldn’t think of anyone more fitting for this award: someone who is new to the European framebuilding scene, a joy to be around, and a caring enough individual to already want to teach others.

Kata, thank you for hanging out all weekend. I’ll forever remember walking home from the techno club with Cala, Konstantin, and you. I hope to see you again sooner rather than later!

@RaschCycles
